Durst
DERST
verb
The archaic past tense of dare, from Old English dorste, preterite of durran, to have courage or boldness; meaning “dared” — had the daring or presumption to do a thing.

Biblical Definition

Durst means “dared” — had the boldness or hardihood for an act — and it appears most often in the KJV as a boundary no man would cross. When the Lord had silenced the Pharisees and Sadducees, “no man was able to answer him a word, neither durst any man from that day forth ask him any more questions” (Mat 22:46): His wisdom raised a fence about Him that daring could not pass. By the sea of Tiberias, before the risen Christ, “none of the disciples durst ask him, Who art thou? knowing that it was the Lord” (Joh 21:12) — holy awe stilling even affectionate curiosity. In Jerusalem, when signs and wonders were done by the apostles’ hands, “of the rest durst no man join himself to them” (Act 5:13): the fear of God on the church held the double-minded at a reverent distance. The word’s most instructive use guards the tongue of an angel: “Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, durst not bring against him a railing accusation, but said, The Lord rebuke thee” (Jud 1:9). If the chief of angels durst not rail even at the devil, how brazen the men who speak evil of dignities they do not understand. Durst marks the edge of holy reverence — the point where daring must yield to fear of the LORD, and the bold man learns there is a line he will not, dare not, pass.

Webster 1828 Definition

The old past tense of “dare” — had the boldness; often marking the line reverence forbids one to cross.

expand to see more

DURST, the archaic preterite of dare: dared; had the courage or presumption.

From Old English dorste, past tense of durran, to have boldness.

None durst ask Christ more questions after His wisdom silenced them (Mat 22:46).

None durst join the awed apostolic church lightly (Act 5:13).

Michael durst not rail even at the devil (Jud 1:9).

Key Scripture

Mat 22:46 — "And no man was able to answer him a word, neither durst any man from that day forth ask him any more questions."

Joh 21:12 — "Jesus saith unto them, Come and dine. And none of the disciples durst ask him, Who art thou? knowing that it was the Lord."

Act 5:13 — "And of the rest durst no man join himself to them: but the people magnified them."

Jud 1:9 — "Yet Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, durst not bring against him a railing accusation, but said, The Lord rebuke thee."

Modern Corruption

Not a contested doctrine but a fading verb; it recovers the vanished sense of reverent fear — the line a wise soul dares not cross.

expand to see more

The word rebukes the brazenness of the age, which durst do anything and reverences nothing. Jude sets the archangel’s restraint against “filthy dreamers” who “speak evil of the things that they know not” (Jud 1:8, 10); if Michael durst not bring a railing accusation against Satan himself, the flippant tongue that mocks God, mocks His ministers, and jeers at every dignity has lost the very organ of the fear of God. What men now call boldness is often only the death of reverence.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is holy dread — that there are questions the awed heart durst not ask and words it durst not speak, not from cowardice but from the fear of the LORD. “None durst” is the mark of a people who know Whose presence they are in. The recovery of that word would restore the recovery of that fear, which is the beginning of wisdom (Pro 9:10).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The archaic past tense of dare, “durst” marks in the KJV the boundary that reverence and the fear of God forbid.

expand to see more

Durst — Old English dorste, preterite of durran, to dare.

It means “dared” — had the boldness or hardihood.

None durst question Christ after His wisdom silenced them (Mat 22:46).

The awe of God held men from lightly joining the church (Act 5:13).

Michael durst not rail even at the devil, but said, The Lord rebuke thee (Jud 1:9).

Usage

"None durst ask Him, for they knew that it was the Lord."

"If the archangel durst not rail at Satan, how brazen the mocking tongue."

"Durst marks the edge where daring must yield to the fear of God."
